analysis.one_liner: Cuts mercury emissions from power plants, industrial boilers, incinerators, chlorine and cement plants by 90% or more, and phases mercury out of everyday products.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Sen. Patrick Leahy with one Republican cosponsor in February 2003, the bill went no further than the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Clean Air Act to require power plants, industrial boilers, waste incinerators, chlorine plants, and cement kilns to slash mercury emissions — at least 90% below 1999 levels for power plants and boilers, and 95% below baseline for chlorine and cement plants [S2]. It would have required permits, quarterly monitoring reports, and annual public release of each facility's mercury emissions, banned emission credit trading between power plants at different sites, and mandated safe disposal of captured mercury [S3]. Beyond smokestacks, it would have required labeling and eventual phaseout of mercury-containing products like fluorescent bulbs, batteries, and thermostats, banned sale of the national defense stockpile of mercury, and funded nationwide monitoring of mercury falling into lakes and streams [S2]. The Senate bill cited federal health data showing about 1 in 12 women of childbearing age had mercury levels above the EPA safety threshold, putting roughly 320,000 newborns a year at risk of neurological effects [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the main beneficiaries would have been women of childbearing age, developing fetuses, children, and people who eat a lot of freshwater fish — the groups the bill's own findings identify as most at risk from mercury, especially through contaminated fish [S3]. Communities downwind of coal-fired power plants in the Great Lakes, Ohio Valley, Northeast, and Gulf Coast regions would have seen the largest emission cuts, and the ban on trading pollution credits between power plant sites meant local residents near the dirtiest plants would get real local reductions rather than watching a distant plant buy the right to keep polluting [S3]. People living near chlor-alkali plants and cement kilns, which the bill targeted for 95% reductions, and households disposing of mercury-containing batteries and bulbs would also have benefited [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fish eaters, pregnant women, children, lake communities

how_it_helps.text: Requires coal- and oil-fired power plants and industrial boilers to cut total mercury emissions by at least 90% from 1999 levels, with facility-specific permits and monitoring results submitted to regulators at least every 90 days [S3].

Bans trading of mercury emission credits between power plants at different sites, so local communities near polluting plants would get real local reductions rather than buying their way out of the problem [S3].

Requires chlor-alkali plants and Portland cement plants to cut their annual mercury emissions by at least 95% below their baseline, two industrial source categories that had largely escaped mercury-specific controls [S3].

Requires mercury-containing products like fluorescent bulbs, batteries, thermostats, and medical instruments to be labeled, separated from the waste stream, and eventually phased out of sale unless the manufacturer proves no mercury-free alternative is available at reasonable cost [S3].

Prohibits sale of the federal National Defense Stockpile mercury for commercial or industrial use, keeping a large surplus of the metal from re-entering commerce, and funds nationwide monitoring of mercury falling from the atmosphere into lakes and waterways [S3].
Mandates annual public reporting of facility-specific mercury emissions for every covered plant, giving communities near polluters direct access to their local plant's numbers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The cost would have fallen on the operators of coal- and oil-fired power plants, industrial boilers, chlor-alkali plants, cement plants, and incinerators, which would have had to install controls, monitor emissions quarterly, and cut output of mercury by 90–95% [S3]. Some of those compliance costs would have been passed to electricity ratepayers and to buyers of cement and industrial products. Manufacturers and importers of mercury-containing products — batteries, fluorescent bulbs, thermostats, medical instruments — would have faced labeling, take-back, and phaseout requirements, and solid-waste handlers would have needed to run separation and removal plans for listed items [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Power plants, cement and chlorine plants, product makers

drawbacks.text: Requiring coal- and oil-fired power plants and boilers to cut mercury emissions 90% from 1999 levels would have imposed substantial compliance costs on utilities, which could have been passed through to electricity customers, particularly in coal-reliant regions.

The three-year prohibition on selling any mercury-containing product without an EPA exemption was a broad mandate that would have forced manufacturers of items like fluorescent bulbs, thermostats, and button-cell batteries to redesign, relabel, or withdraw products, and exemptions required a public hearing process plus manufacturer-funded take-back programs [S3].

The waste-stream provisions — separation and removal plans for anyone transferring solid waste, labeling requirements, and a 0.080 mg/dscm emission ceiling for incinerators — would have added ongoing monitoring, reporting, and infrastructure costs for municipal and private waste handlers, including small municipal incinerator operators.

The bill gave the EPA Administrator considerable discretion in setting the actual standards, baselines, and exemptions within 180 days, leaving much of the real-world stringency — and the cost burden — to be determined by the agency's rulemaking rather than by Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health case was strong: the bill built its targets on the National Academy of Sciences 2000 report and the EPA's own inventory of major mercury sources, and it addressed a documented and growing problem — fish advisories had risen from 899 in 1993 to 2,073 in 1999, and 44 states issued mercury advisories in 2002 [S3]. The real costs are the compliance bills: a 90% cut from power plants and boilers would have required significant pollution-control capital at aging coal plants, some of which would have flowed to electricity customers, and the near-total 95% cuts at chlor-alkali and cement plants were aggressive relative to what those industries had ever been required to do [S3]. The product phaseout is broad — it bans sale of any mercury-containing product without an exemption — and the waste-sector planning and labeling requirements add paperwork costs throughout the solid-waste system [S3]. An honest weighing comes down on the public side: mercury is a potent neurotoxin with no safe exposure level for fetal development, the technology to capture it was available, and the bill explicitly directed EPA to authorize cost-effective control methods rather than dictate specific equipment [S3]. The bill died without any committee action, so these costs were never formally weighed against the benefits in Congress.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it along to the Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced in February 2003, and it sat there through the end of the 108th Congress without ever being taken up.

narrative.text: The bill's complete action history consists of three steps on a single day: introduction, introductory remarks by the sponsor, and a referral to the Committee on Environment and Public Works — nothing further through January 3, 2005 [S5].
The bill drew two sponsors in total — Sen. Leahy and one Republican cosponsor — giving it bipartisan sponsorship but no broad base of support to move it [S4].

The bill was not a narrow measure: it would have set binding emission-reduction floors (90% for power plants and boilers, 95% for chlor-alkali and cement plants), created permit, monitoring, and public reporting requirements, banned cross-site emission trading, phased mercury out of consumer products, and halted sale of the federal mercury stockpile [S2].

The findings in the bill text documented the scale of the problem it targeted: 44 states issued mercury fish advisories in 2002 versus 27 in 1993, national advisories rose 131% from 1993 to 1999, and roughly 4.9 million women of childbearing age had mercury levels above EPA's safety threshold [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-burning power plants, chlor-alkali and cement plants, mercury-product manufacturers, and waste incinerator operators were better off — they avoided the cost of deep mercury emission cuts and continued operating without a federal mercury-specific mandate. Electric customers and people who eat fish from contaminated waterways were worse off, absorbing continued mercury exposure.

for.name: Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 27, 2003 and delivered introductory remarks on the floor (CR S2941-2942) [S5].

for.name: Olympia Snowe
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor, making it a bipartisan two-senator effort [S4].

against.name: James Inhofe
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that received the bill and never scheduled a hearing or markup on it, letting it die in committee when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, but it never reached a floor vote or committee vote, so the record shows no partisan split — only that a committee run by the majority party took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill would have forced a 90% cut in mercury emissions from 1999 levels, with permits, quarterly monitoring reports, and an annual public report of each plant's emissions [S3]. The industry had never faced a mercury-specific federal mandate of this scale; avoiding it meant avoiding major pollution-control spending, some share of which would otherwise have been recovered through electricity rates.

industries.industry: Mercury-cell chlor-alkali plants (chlorine and caustic soda producers)
industries.note: Each plant would have had to cut annual mercury emissions at least 95% below its baseline — effectively forcing a shift away from the mercury-cell production process itself [S3]. The small number of US plants still using that process had operated for decades under looser requirements.

The bill would have required kilns and other plant operations to cut mercury emissions 95% below baseline and obtain permits [S3]. Cement kilns are a significant mercury source that would otherwise have gone unaddressed.

industries.industry: Manufacturers and importers of mercury-containing products (batteries, fluorescent bulbs, thermostats, switches, medical instruments)
industries.note: Products would need mercury-content labeling, and three years after enactment any mercury-containing product could not be sold without an EPA exemption proving the use was essential and no reasonable mercury-free alternative existed [S3]. This would push the industry toward mercury-free redesigns.

industries.industry: Solid waste, medical waste, and hazardous waste incineration operators
industries.note: Operators would face mandatory mercury monitoring, 90-day reporting, an enforceable emission ceiling of 0.080 mg per dry standard cubic meter, and installation of controls reaching 0.060 mg if they missed it, plus separation-and-removal plans for waste feed streams [S3]. The costs would fall partly on private operators and partly on municipal facilities serving local taxpayers.

industries.industry: Mercury stockpile holders and mercury traders
industries.note: The bill would have prohibited selling the federal National Defense Stockpile mercury domestically or internationally for commercial use, removing a large supply of the metal from the market [S3].
